title: What Do You Do When Things Go Right?
text:
Much research on relationships asks how partners support each other through hard times. In 2004 Shelly Gable, Harry Reis and their colleagues turned the question around: what happens when one person shares good news?

In a series of studies with students and dating or married couples in the United States, including daily diaries and questionnaires, they looked at how people responded when a partner told them about a positive event, such as a promotion or a good grade. They sorted responses into four types. Active and constructive: enthusiastic interest and questions ("That's wonderful, tell me how it happened"). Passive and constructive: quiet, low-key support. Active and destructive: pointing out the downsides. Passive and destructive: ignoring the news or changing the subject.

Telling others about good events added to people's happiness beyond the event itself. And how partners reacted mattered a great deal. When people felt their partners usually responded in the active, constructive way, they reported more satisfaction, intimacy and trust in the relationship. The other three types of response, including the quietly supportive one, were linked to lower relationship quality. Being there when things go right turned out to be as telling as being there when things go wrong.
lesson: When someone shares good news, respond with real enthusiasm and curious questions. A distracted "that's nice" quietly costs a relationship more than you might think.
people: Shelly Gable, Harry Reis, Emily Impett, Evan Asher
location: University of California, Los Angeles, and University of Rochester, USA
source: Gable, S. L., Reis, H. T., Impett, E. A., and Asher, E. R. (2004). What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(2), 228-245.
